messages.author: d78486bfff620d81
messages.subject: NIMBLE version 1.1.0 released
parts:
We're pleased to announce the release of Version 1.1.0 of NIMBLE. This release provides new functionality as well as various bug fixes and improved error trapping, including:
  • Improving our automatic differentiation (AD) system so it can be used in a wider range of models, including models with stochastic indexing, discrete latent states, and CAR distributions. Support for AD for these models means that HMC sampling and Laplace approximation can be used.
  • Allowing distributions and functions (whether user-defined or built-in) that lack AD support (such as `dinterval`, `dconstraint`, and truncated distributions) to be used and compiled in AD-enabled models. The added flexibility increases the range of models in which one can use AD methods (HMC or Laplace) on some parts of a model and other samplers or methods on other parts.
  • Adding `nimIntegrate` to the NIMBLE language, providing one-dimensional numerical integration via adaptive quadrature, equivalent to R's `integrate`. This can, for example, be used in a user-defined function or distribution for use in model code, such as to implement certain point process or survival models that involve a one-dimensional integral.
  • Adding a "prior samples" MCMC sampler, which uses an existing set of numerical samples to define the prior distribution of model node(s).
  • Better support of the dCRP distribution in non-standard model structures.
  • Adding error trapping to prevent accidental use of  C++ keywords as model variable names.
  • Removing the `RW_multinomial` MCMC sampler, which was found to generate incorrect posterior results (in cases when a latent state followed a multinomial distribution)
  • Fixing a bug in conjugacy checking in a case of subsets of multivariate nodes.
  • Fixing `is.na` and `is.nan` to operate in the expected vectorized fashion.
  • Improving documentation of AD, nimbleHMC, and nimbleSMC in the manual.
  • Updating Eigen (the C++ linear algebra library used by nimble) to version 3.4.0.
Please see the NEWS file in the installed package for more details.

- Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team

messages.author: cd1a27f1af2cf2c5
messages.subject: Re: NIMBLE version 1.1.0 released
parts:
Hi Chris,

I am currently using a model with a multinomial distribution, but I encountered an error message stating that support for sampling multinomial distributions was removed from NIMBLE due to incorrect sampling results.

Is there a corrected version available, or would you recommend using a different sampler?

Thank you for your assistance.

Best regards,

Edel Lheureux

messages.subject: Re: NIMBLE version 1.1.0 released
parts:

One of the challenges is that if N (size) itself is a latent variable that must be sampled by MCMC, it becomes necessary to sample it jointly with the multinomial outcome vector.
Best wishes,
Perry

messages.author: f116cbe5c604c988
messages.subject: Re: NIMBLE version 1.1.0 released
parts:
Heather, I'm sorry it's taken a few days to respond.  Let me try to give a brief view of the landscape regarding your question.

For some period of time, nimble provided a multinomial sampler (internally, called the RW_multinomial sampler; let's call this version of the sampler version A).  One point to understand, given an unobserved multinomial-distributed random variate, the multinomial sampler was capable of redistributing (reallocating) a *fixed* number of total counts (let's say N) over the (also fixed) number of observation categories (let's call this K).  So, concretely, if your model code looks something like this:

code <- nimbleCode({
    ...
    x[1:K] ~ dmulti(prob = p[1:K], size = N)
})

Then, in the case where N is fixed and immutable, the probability vector p[1:K] may be constant, or may itself be assigned a prior distribution (either jointly, or element-wise), K is also fixed, and we wish to sample different ways that the (fixed) number of N observation counts can be distributed among the K categories - the multinomial would accomplish this.  (main point being: it would be a different problem to also allow N to be mutable; the multinomial sampler can not / does not handle that more general case).

Version A of the multinomial sampler, as formerly present in the package, had several features:
- The internal adaptation may generally not scale well to large problems
- The internal adaptation was not founded in published theory
- Adaptation aside, version A of the sampler contained a bug, causing incorrect results

Realizing the above, version A of the multinomial sampler was removed from the package within the past year or so.

Because of this new void, on a separate branch of the nimble package, we went ahead and fixed the (only known) bug in the multinomial sampler.  Let's call the fixed sampler version B of the multinomial sampler.  The fixed version of the sampler, version B, is available on a GitHub branch called "multinomial_sampler".  If you want to use it, you can install a version of nimble which provides version B of the multinomial sampler using the code below:

remove.packages("nimble")
library(remotes)
remotes::install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "multinomial_sampler", subdir = "packages/nimble")
library(nimble)

We (the development team) have a goal to re-introduce a simpler version of the multinomial sampler (let's call this version C) back into the package.  Features of version C of the multinomial sampler will / would be:
- The performance of version C would scale better to large problems
- The implementation of version C would be completely grounded on published theory
- Version C of the sampler would not contain any bugs

With any luck, this updated version C of the multinomial sampler would be introduced into an upcoming nimble release.  And for now, you can use version B of the sampler, using the code above to install nimble from the "multinomial_sampler" branch.

I hope this provides a helpful view of the landscape regarding your question, and helps get you moving forward.

Cheers,
Daniel
